Moscow State University: Lomonosov Moscow State University (MSU; Russian: Московский государственный университет имени М. В. Ломоносова, often abbreviated МГУ) is coeducational public research university located in Moscow, Russia. founded January 25, 1755 by Mikhail Lomonosov. MSU renamed after Lomonosov in 1940 then known as "Lomonosov University". houses tallest educational building in world. rated among universities with best reputation in world. current rector is Viktor Sadovnichiy.
 Sergei Aleksandrovich Tokarev: Sergei Aleksandrovich Tokarev (Russian: Серге́й Алекса́ндрович То́карев, 29 December 1899 – 19 April 1985) was Russian scholar, ethnographer, historian researcher of religious beliefs doctor of historical sciences, professor at Moscow State University.
 Sergei Kosarev: Sergei Aleksandrovich Kosarev (Russian: Серге́й Александрович Косарев ; born January 29, 1993) Russian football midfielder currently plays for FC MITOS Novocherkassk.
 Sergei Sholokhov: Sergei Aleksandrovich Sholokhov (Russian: Серге́й Александрович Шолохов ; born September 6, 1980) Russian professional football player. As of August 2009, plays in Russian Second Division for FC Avangard Kursk. Before 2004 known as Sergei Kocherga (Russian: Серге́й Кочерга
 Sergei Dmitrochenko: Sergei Aleksandrovich Dmitrochenko (Russian: Серге́й Александрович Дмитроченко ; born June 21, 1993) is Russian football midfielder.

Halina Reijn: Halina Reijn (born 10 November 1975) is a Dutch actress and writer.
 Black Book (film): Black Book (Dutch: Zwartboek ) is a 2006 Dutch thriller film co-written and directed by Paul Verhoeven starring Carice van Houten, Sebastian Koch, Thom Hoffman, and Halina Reijn. film, credited as based on several true events and characters, is about a young Jewish woman in Netherlands who becomes a spy for resistance during World War II after tragedy befalls her in encounter with Nazis. film had world premiere on 1 September 2006 at Venice Film Festival and public release on 14 September 2006 in Netherlands. first film Verhoeven made in Netherlands since "The Fourth Man," made in 1983 before he moved to United States.
 Black Book (novel): Black Book (Dutch: Zwartboek ) is a Dutch-language 2006 thriller novel by Laurens Abbink Spaink. It is novelization of Dutch film "Black Book" (2006). tells the story of a young Jewish woman, Rachel Stein, and her struggle for survival during and after the Second World War. book has a photo section, and afterword by Paul Verhoeven and Gerard Soeteman.
 Black Book (World War II): The Black Book: The Ruthless Murder of Jews by German-Fascist Invaders Throughout Temporarily-Occupied Regions of Soviet Union and in German Nazi Death Camps established on occupied Polish soil during War 1941–1945 alternatively The Black Book of the Holocaust, or simply The Black Book (Russian: Чёрная Книга , "Chornaya Kniga"; Yiddish: דאָס שוואַרצע בוך , "Dos shvartse bukh"), was a result of collaborative effort by Jewish Anti-Fascist Committee (JAC) and members of American Jewish community to document anti-Jewish crimes of the Holocaust and participation of Jews in fighting and resistance movement against Nazis during World War II.
Black Book (non-standard disc format): Black Book is an unofficial designation of optical disc (OD) formats that defy official standards for CD, DVD, HD DVD and Blu-ray Discs. Most formats considered Black Book are formats used for video games or Digital Rights Management.
 Black Book of the Admiralty: The Black Book of the Admiralty is a compilation of English admiralty law created over of several English monarchs' reigns, including most important decisions of the High Court of Admiralty. Its starting point is Rolls of Oléron, promulgated in c 1160 by Eleanor of Aquitaine, although the "Black Book" is undoubtedly later. book states High Court of Admiralty was established during reign of Edward I (1272–1307), although more recent scholarship places establishment at c. 1360 during reign of Edward III. Apart from Rolls of Oléron, earliest statute referred to is the "Liber memorandorum" (1338), of a separate manuscript copy is available in archives of City of London.

American Beauty (1999 film): American Beauty is a 1999 American drama film directed by Sam Mendes written by Alan Ball. Kevin Spacey stars as Lester Burnham, a 42-year-old advertising executive who has a midlife crisis when he becomes infatuated with his teenage daughter's best friend, Angela (Mena Suvari). Annette Bening co-stars as Lester's materialistic wife, Carolyn, and Thora Birch plays their insecure daughter, Jane. Wes Bentley, Chris Cooper, and Allison Janney also feature. film is described by academics as satire of American middle-class notions of beauty and personal satisfaction; analysis focused on film's explorations of romantic, and paternal love, sexuality, beauty, materialism, self-liberation, and redemption.
 American Beauty (1927 film): American Beauty is a lost 1927 American silent film romantic drama produced and distributed by First National Pictures. film directed by Richard Wallace starred Billie Dove. based on short story "American Beauty" by Wallace Irwin. She supported by Walter McGrail and Margaret Livingston.
 American Beauty (soundtrack): American Beauty: Music from Original Motion Picture Soundtrack is the soundtrack album to the 1999 film starring Kevin Spacey and Annette Bening.
 Christopher Greenbury: Christopher Greenbury, ACE (September 24, 1951 – January 4, 2007) was a British film editor with more than thirty film credits dating from 1979's "The Muppet Movie". With Tariq Anwar, won BAFTA Award for Best Editing for "American Beauty" (1999), also nominated for an Academy Award for Best Film Editing. "American Beauty" is a serious drama, but in general Greenbury edited comedy films, including six directed by the Farrelly brothers commencing with 1994's "Dumb and Dumber".
 La Belle Américaine: La Belle Américaine English: The American Beauty , is a French comedy film from 1961, directed by Robert Dhéry, written by Alfred Adam, starring Alfred Adam and Louis de Funès.film known under the titles: "La bella americana" (Italy), "The American Beauty" (English title), "Der tolle Amerikaner" (West Germany).
 American Beauty/American Psycho Tour: The American Beauty/American Psycho Tour was a concert tour by American rock band Fall Out Boy. Supporting the band's sixth studio album "American Beauty/American Psycho" (2015), tour visited North America and Europe in 2015. North American leg co-headlined with American rapper Wiz Khalifa under the name The Boys of Zummer. Boys of Zummer leg with Wiz Khalifa ranked fifty-ninth for Pollstar's Year End Top 200 North American Tours of 2015, grossing $18.2 million.

Florida Senate: The Florida Senate is the upper house of the legislature of the U.S. state of Florida. Along with the House of Representatives, it composes the Florida Legislature. The Senate has 40 members, each elected from a single-member district with a population of about 470,000. The Senate meets at the State Capitol in Tallahassee.
 Ken Pruitt: Ken Pruitt (born January 24, 1957) was a Republican member of the Florida Senate, representing the 28th District from 2000 to 2009. His district includes portions of Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie Counties. He was previously a member of the Florida House of Representatives from 1990 through 2000.
 Nevada Legislature: The Nevada Legislature is the state legislature of the U.S. state of Nevada. Legislature is a bicameral body, consisting of the lower house Nevada Assembly, with 42 members, and the upper house Nevada Senate, with 21 members. All 63 members of Legislature are elected from an equal amount of constituent districts across the state. The Legislature is the third smallest bicameral state legislature in the United States (the Alaska Legislature is the smallest bicameral, with only 60 members and the Delaware General Assembly has 62 members).
 Alaska Legislature: The Alaska Legislature is the state legislature of the U.S. state of Alaska. It is a bicameral institution, consisting of the lower Alaska House of Representatives, with 40 members, and the upper house Alaska Senate, with 20 members. There are 40 House Districts (1-40) and 20 Senate Districts (A-T). With a total of 60 lawmakers, the Alaska Legislature is the smallest bicameral state legislature in the United States and the second-smallest of all state legislatures (only the 49-member unicameral Nebraska Legislature is smaller). are no term limits for either chamber.
 Upper house: An upper house, sometimes called a Senate, is one of two chambers of a bicameral legislature (or one of three chambers of a tricameral legislature), the other chamber being the lower house.The house formally designated as the upper house is usually smaller, and often has more restricted power, than the lower house. Examples of upper houses in countries include the UK's House of Lords, India's Rajya Sabha, Russia's Federation Council, Ireland's Seanad, Germany's Bundesrat and the United States Senate.
 Wisconsin Legislature: The Wisconsin Legislature is the state legislature of the U.S. state of Wisconsin. The Legislature is a bicameral body composed of the upper house Wisconsin State Senate and lower Wisconsin State Assembly, both of which have had Republican majorities since January 2011. With both houses combined, legislature has 132 members representing an equal number of constituent districts. The Legislature convenes at the state capitol in Madison.

Calibanus: Calibanus is a genus of two species of flowering plants, both evergreen succulents from dry areas of northeastern Mexico. The APG III classification system places it in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Nolinoideae (formerly family Ruscaceae. ) It was formerly included in the Agavaceae (now Agavoideae) but is now separated from them, for it is polycarpic and dioecious. Its name refers to the monster Caliban, an antagonist in Shakespeare's "The Tempest".
 Greyia: Greyia is a genus of plant in family Melianthaceae. It contains three species:
 Banksiamyces: Banksiamyces is a genus of fungi in the order Helotiales, with a tentative placement in the family Helotiaceae. genus contains four species, grow on the seed follicles of dead infructescences or "cones" of various species of "Banksia", a genus in the plant family Proteaceae endemic to Australia. Fruit bodies of the fungus appear as small (typically less than 10 mm diameter), shallow dark cups on the follicles of the "Banksia" fruit. edges of dry fruit bodies fold inwards, appearing like narrow slits. first specimens of "Banksiamyces", known then as "Tympanis toomansis", were described in 1887. Specimens continued to be collected occasionally for almost 100 years before becoming examined more critically in the early 1980s, leading to the creation of a new genus to contain determined to be three distinct species, "B. katerinae", "B. macrocarpus", and "B. toomansis". A fourth species, "B. maccannii", was added in 1984.
 Megalurus: Megalurus is a genus of passerine bird in the family Locustellidae. genus was once placed in the Old World warbler "wastebin" family Sylviidae. genus contains six species also known as the typical grassbirds.The genus is distributed from northern China and Japan, to India in west, and Australia in the south, with most species located wholly or partly in the tropics. genus is also sometimes considered to include the genus "Bowdleria", which holds the fernbirds of New Zealand. The most widespread species, the tawny grassbird, ranges from the Philippines to southern New South Wales, whereas the Fly River grassbird is restricted to swampland in the southern part of New Guinea. natural habitat of typical grassbirds is, as name suggests, wet grasslands, swamps and other marshlands. Some species exist away from water in tall grasslands, heathlands, and forest clearings. Some species have adapted to the margins of rice fields and gardens.
 Lophodermium: Lophodermium is a genus of fungi within the family Rhytismataceae. genus contains 145 species and has a global distribution. Species of this genus are usually observed producing zone lines, conidiomata and ascomata on dead fallen leaves, but at least some are known to colonize living leaves. In many cases they then live inside the colonized leaf as a symptomless endobiont, where they are regarded as detritivores utilising dead plant matter. In a few cases they may kill all or part of the leaf prematurely, and is substantial literature dealing with those species as plant pathogens. genus infects many different plant families but with a notable concentration in the family Pinaceae; many "Lophodermium" species are restricted to a single host genus (or even species), but some, particularly those infecting grasses, may infect several genera. Some are economically important plant pathogens, such as those that cause needlecast disease in European Black Pine, Scots Pine and Red Pine in forestry and christmas tree plantations. In these species, notably "L. pinastri" and "L. seditiosum", fungal spores disperse and infect pine needles in late summer, which turn brown by the following spring and then fall off.

John Updike: John Hoyer Updike (March 18, 1932 – January 27, 2009) was an American novelist, poet, short story writer, art critic, literary critic. One of three writers to win Pulitzer Prize for Fiction more than once (the others were Booth Tarkington and William Faulkner), Updike published twenty novels, a dozen short-story collections, poetry, art and literary criticism children's books during career.
 Tom Clancy: Thomas Leo "Tom" Clancy Jr. (April 12, 1947 – October 1, 2013) was American novelist known for his technically detailed espionage and military-science story lines set during and after Cold War. Seventeen his novels were bestsellers, more than 100 million copies of his books in print. His name also used on movie scripts written by ghost writers, nonfiction books on military subjects, video games. was part-owner of Baltimore Orioles vice-chairman of their community activities and public affairs committees.
 Tom Clancy's Rainbow 6: Patriots: Tom Clancy's Rainbow 6: Patriots is a cancelled first-person shooter video game, part of "Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six" series, announced on cover of December 2011 issue of "Game Informer". published by Ubisoft developed by company's Montreal studio, with additional development by Ubisoft Toronto and Red Storm Entertainment. Due to death of Tom Clancy in October 2013, concern raised this game would become last to bear his name. Ubisoft stated will continue putting Tom Clancy's name on future Tom Clancy titles out of respect for late author.
 Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon 2: Summit Strike: Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon 2: Summit Strike is expansion to "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon 2". several minor differences between "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon 2: Summit Strike", and "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon 2". most notable being the difficulty, Summit Strike regarded as harder of two.differences include new multiplayer modes, such as Heli Hunt.

Benedict Arnold: Benedict Arnold (January 14, 1741 [O.S. January 3, 1740] June 14, 1801) was a general during American Revolutionary War, fought for American Continental Army later defected to British Army. While general on American side obtained command of fortifications at West Point, New York (which after 1802 would become site of U.S. Military Academy), overlooking cliffs at Hudson River (upriver from British-occupied New York City), planned to surrender them to British forces. plan exposed in September 1780. commissioned into British Army as a brigadier general.
 John André: John André (2 May 1750 – 2 October 1780) was a British Army officer hanged as a spy by Continental Army during American Revolutionary War for assisting Benedict Arnold's attempted surrender of fort at West Point, New York to British.
 Benjamin Lincoln: Benjamin Lincoln (January 24, 1733 (O.S. January 13, 1732) – May 9, 1810) was an American army officer. served as major general in Continental Army during American Revolutionary War. Lincoln notable for involved in three major surrenders during war: participation in Battles of Saratoga contributed to John Burgoyne's surrender of British army, oversaw largest American surrender of war at 1780 Siege of Charleston, as George Washington's second in command accepted British surrender at Yorktown.
 Siege of Yorktown: The Siege of Yorktown, also known as the Battle of Yorktown, the Surrender at Yorktown, German Battle or the Siege of Little York, ending on October 19, 1781, at Yorktown, Virginia, was decisive victory by combined force of American Continental Army troops led by General George Washington and French Army troops led by Comte de Rochambeau over British Army commanded by British peer and Lieutenant General Charles Cornwallis.culmination of Yorktown campaign, siege proved to last major land battle of American Revolutionary War in North American theater, as surrender by Cornwallis, and capture of both him and his army, prompted British government to negotiate end to conflict. battle boosted faltering American morale and revived French enthusiasm for war, undermining popular support for conflict in Great Britain.
 Battle of Germantown: Battle of Germantown was major engagement in Philadelphia campaign of American Revolutionary War. fought on October 4, 1777, at Germantown, Pennsylvania, between British Army led by Sir William Howe, and American Continental Army, with 2nd Canadian Regiment, under George Washington.
 Board of War: Board of War, also known as Board of War and Ordnance, created by Second Continental Congress as special standing committee to oversee American Continental Army's administration and to make recommendations regarding army to Congress. On January 24, 1776, Congressional delegate Edward Rutledge, echoing Gen. George Washington's concerns, suggested war office similar to Britain's be established. Pressure from Washington and large volume of military business led Congress to establish Board of War and Ordnance on June 12, 1776. Five delegates of Congress, initially John Adams, Roger Sherman, Benjamin Harrison, James Wilson, and Edward Rutledge, assisted by permanent secretary, Richard Peters, composed Board of War. assumed responsibilities for compiling master roster of all Continental Army officers; monitoring returns of all troops, arms, and equipment; maintaining correspondence files; securing prisoners of war. Board of War began functioning on June 21, 1776.

Salma Hayek: Salma Hayek Pinault ( Hayek Jiménez) (born September 2, 1966), known professionally as Salma Hayek, is a Mexican and American film actress, producer, and former model. began career in Mexico starring in telenovela "Teresa" starred in film "El Callejón de los Milagros" ("Miracle Alley") for nominated for an Ariel Award. In 1991 Hayek moved to Hollywood came to prominence with roles in movies "Desperado" (1995), "From Dusk Till Dawn" (1996), "Dogma" (1999), "Wild Wild West" (1999).
 Ethel Houbiers: Ethel Houbiers is a French voice actress. French voice of Penélope Cruz and Salma Hayek.
 Roger Carel: Roger Carel (born Roger Bancharel; 14 August 1927) is a French actor and voice talent, known for recurring film roles as Asterix, French voice of "Star Wars'" C-3PO, and French voice of "Winnie the Pooh". also dubbing David Suchet as Hercule Poirot in Agatha Christie's Poirot. voiced Wally Gator, Mickey Mouse and Woody Woodpecker in French. born in Paris, France.
 Emmanuel Curtil: Emmanuel Curtil (born 7 February 1971) is a French actor known primarily for voice work dubbed voice of Matthew Perry (Chandler) for first eight seasons of American sitcom "Friends". Curtil is also "French voice" of Jim Carrey. also current voice of Goofy, assuming duty from Gérard Rinaldi, who died in 2012.
 Dorothée Jemma: Dorothée Jemma (born June 16, 1956) is a French voice actress specializing in dubbing. dub voice of Jennifer Aniston, Melanie Griffith and Sheryl Lee.
 Bernard Alane: Bernard Alane (born Bernard Noël Vetel 25 December 1948 in Paris) is French actor and singer, son of actress Annick Alane.best known in France for his roles in two films directed by Edouard Molinaro, "Hibernatus" and "Mon oncle Benjamin", but achieved better fame as voice actor, practically in dubbing. official French voice of Stanley Tucci and Ray Liotta.

Croydon Airport: Croydon Airport (ICAO: EGCR ) was an airport in South London, England. was main airport for London before replaced by Northolt Aerodrome, London Heathrow Airport and Gatwick Airport. terminal building and entrance lodge are Grade II listed buildings.
 Gatwick Airport: Gatwick Airport (also known as London Gatwick) (IATA: LGW, ICAO: EGKK) is major international airport in south-east England, 29.5 mi south of Central London and 2.7 NM north of Crawley. second-busiest airport by total passenger traffic in United Kingdom, after London Heathrow. Gatwick is eighth-busiest airport in Europe. Until 2016, was busiest single-use runway airport in world before overtaken by Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport.
 Grantley Adams International Airport: Grantley Adams International Airport (GAIA) (IATA: BGI, ICAO: TBPB) is international airport of Barbados, located in Seawell, Christ Church. only designated port of entry for persons arriving and departing by air in Barbados operates as major gateway to Eastern Caribbean. airport has direct service to destinations in United States, Canada, Central America and Europe and serves as second hub for LIAT. In 2016, airport was 8th busiest airport in Caribbean region; and third busiest airport in Lesser Antilles; after Queen Beatrix International Airport in Aruba, and Pointe-à-Pitre International Airport in Republic of France within island of Guadeloupe. GAIA, remains important air-link for cruise ship passengers departing and arriving at Port of Bridgetown, and base of operations for Regional Security System (RSS), and Regional (Caribbean) Police Training Centre.
 Heathrow Airport: Heathrow Airport (also known as London Heathrow) (IATA: LHR, ICAO: EGLL) is a major international airport in London, United Kingdom.Heathrow is second busiest airport in world by international passenger traffic (surpassed by Dubai International in 2014), busiest airport in Europe by passenger traffic, and seventh busiest airport in world by total passenger traffic. In 2016, it handled record 75.7 million passengers, a 1.0% increase from 2015.
 Athens International Airport: Athens International Airport "Eleftherios Venizelos" (Greek: Διεθνής Αερολιμένας Αθηνών «Ελευθέριος Βενιζέλος» , "Diethnís Aeroliménas Athinón "Elefthérios Venizélos"") (IATA: ATH, ICAO: LGAV) , commonly initialized as "AIA", began operation on 28 March 2001 is primary international airport serves city of Athens and region of Attica. It is Greece's busiest airport and serves as hub and main base of Aegean Airlines other Greek airlines. airport is currently in Group 2 of Airports Council International (10–25 million) and as of 2016, Athens International is 27th busiest airport in Europe.
 Dublin Airport: Dublin Airport, (Irish: Aerfort Bhaile Átha Cliath ) (IATA: DUB, ICAO: EIDW) , is international airport serving Dublin, capital city of Ireland. operated by DAA (formerly Dublin Airport Authority). airport located 5.4 nmi north of Dublin in Collinstown, Fingal. In 2016, 27.9 million passengers passed through airport, making it airport's busiest year on record. 15th busiest airport in Europe, and also busiest of state's airports by total passenger traffic. has greatest traffic levels on the island of Ireland, followed by Belfast International Airport, County Antrim.

Cairnburgh Castle: Cairnburgh Castle is a ruined castle located on islands of Cairn na Burgh Mòr and Cairn na Burgh Beag, Argyll and Bute, Scotland. These islands are at northern extremity of the Treshnish Isles at the mouth of Loch Tuath, Mull north of Iona. 1991's "The Changing Scottish Landscape" characterizes it as "one of the most isolated fortifications in Britain...[and] also one of the strangest."
 Isabella Kelly: Isabella Kelly, née Fordyce, also Isabella Hedgeland (born at Cairnburgh Castle in Scottish Highlands and baptised on 4 May 1759 – died on 25 June 1857 in London) was a Scottish novelist and poet.
 Clun Castle: Clun Castle is a ruined castle in small town of Clun, Shropshire. Clun Castle was established by Norman lord Robert de Say after Norman invasion of England and on to become an important Marcher lord castle in the 12th century, with an extensive castle-guard system. Owned for years by the Fitzalan family, Clun played key part in protecting region from Welsh attack until it gradually abandoned as a property in favour of more luxurious Arundel Castle. Fitzalans converted Clun Castle into a hunting lodge in 14th century, complete with pleasure gardens, but by 16th century castle was largely ruined. Slighted in 1646 after English Civil War Clun remained in poor condition until renovation work in 1890s.
 Scharfenstein Castle (Kiedrich): Scharfenstein Castle (German: "Burg Scharfenstein" ), a ruined castle near town of Kiedrich in Hesse, Germany, was part of the Bishopric of Mainz’s border fortifications. erected in 1160 under Christian I (Archbishop of Mainz).
 Castillo de Tabernas: Castillo de Tabernas is a ruined castle on outskirts of municipality of Tabernas, Almería province, in autonomous community of Andalusia, Spain.It built in the 11th century during time of Arab domination. It is of Moorish style and situated on top of a hill. When it was built, it occupied entire hill, though currently only a part is preserved. In 1993, it declared a Bien de Interés Cultural monument. During siege of Almeria, Ferdinand and Isabella ensconced themselves in the castle.

Naval Submarine Base New London: New London is United States Navy's primary East Coast submarine base, also known as the "Home of the Submarine Force". located in Groton, Connecticut.
 Robert Croft (diver): Robert Croft is a free-diver in 1967, became first person to free-dive beyond depth of 200 feet. Croft was US Navy diving instructor in 1962 at US Naval Submarine Base New London submarine school in Groton, Connecticut. At submarine escape training tank, instructors train prospective submariners how to escape from a disabled submarine on sea bottom.
 Naval Consolidated Brig, Miramar: Naval Consolidated Brig, Miramar (NAVCONBRIG) is a military prison operated by U.S. Navy at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in Miramar, San Diego, California, under 10 mi north of downtown San Diego. one of three Navy consolidated brigs the Pacific area regional confinement facility for United States Department of Defense. also known as the Joint Regional Correctional Facility Southwest. 208000 sqft facility has capacity of up to 400 male and female prisoners staffed with 31 civilian and 173 military personnel.
 RAF Croft: Royal Air Force Croft or RAF Croft is a former Royal Air Force station located 4.6 mi south of Darlington, County Durham, England 8 mi north east of Richmond, North Yorkshire. site also known locally as Croft Aerodrome or Neasham.
 Tomb Raider: Tomb Raider, also known as Lara Croft: Tomb Raider between 2001 and 2007, is a media franchise originated with action-adventure video game series created by British gaming company Core Design. Formerly owned by Eidos Interactive, then by Square Enix after acquisition of Eidos in 2009, franchise focuses on fictional English archaeologist Lara Croft, travels around world searching for lost artifacts and infiltrating dangerous tombs and ruins.gameplay focuses around action-adventure exploration of environments, solving puzzles navigating hostile environments filled with traps fighting numerous enemies. Additional media grown up around theme in form of film adaptations, comics novels.
 Lara Croft: Tomb Raider: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider (also known as simply Tomb Raider) is a 2001 action-adventure film based on popular "Tomb Raider" video game series featuring character Lara Croft portrayed by Angelina Jolie. international co-production between United States, United Kingdom, Japan, Germany, directed by Simon West revolves around Lara Croft trying to obtain ancient artifacts from enemy, Illuminati.
 John Ellis Roosevelt Estate: John Ellis Roosevelt Estate, also known as Meadow Croft, is a historic estate located at Sayville in Suffolk County, New York. main house, roughly L-shaped, is composed of two distinct parts: original farmhouse, built about 1850, and now rear of the house; and larger, more formal Colonial Revival mansion built 1891-1892 set perpendicular to it. original section is a two-story, rectangular farmhouse, sheathed in clapboard surmounted by gable roof. 1891–92 section is a clapboarded, two-story structure with elaborate facade with generous porch surmounted by steeply pitched, truncated hipped roof. Also on property are contributing carriage house, equipment barn, garage, caretaker's cottage, swimming pool, storage hut, archaeological sites. property purchased by Robert Barnwell Roosevelt (1829–1906) in 1873; his son John Ellis Roosevelt (1853–1939) commissioned the estate.

Believe (Jai McDowall album): Believe is the debut studio album by Scottish singer and "Britain's Got Talent" winner Jai McDowall. album was released on 9 December 2011 via Sony Music and Syco Music. A promotional single, "With or Without You" was released and performed on various UK shows such as "Daybreak".
 With or Without You: "With or Without You" is a song by Irish rock band U2. It is the third track from their fifth studio album, "The Joshua Tree" (1987), and released as the album's lead single on 16 March 1987. song was the group's most successful single at the time, becoming their first number-one hit in both the United States and Canada by topping the "Billboard" Hot 100 for three weeks and the "RPM" national singles chart for one week, with a further three weeks at number two.
 The Fly (song): "The Fly" is a song by Irish rock band U2. It is seventh track from their 1991 album, "Achtung Baby", and released as the album's first single on 21 October 1991. "The Fly" introduced a more abrasive sounding U2, song featured danceable hip-hop beats, industrial textures, distorted vocals, and an elaborate guitar solo. Lead vocalist Bono described the song as "the sound of four men chopping down "The Joshua Tree"," due to its departure from the traditional sound that had characterised the band in the 1980s.
 Bill Grainer: Bill Grainer is a Grammy certified American songwriter and producer. He has written for such artists as Jai McDowall, Linda Eder, and Jennifer Hudson, with whom he co-wrote the song "Stand Up" for her Grammy Award-winning self-titled debut album.
 Heartbeat (The Fray song): "Heartbeat" is the first single from The Fray's third album "Scars & Stories". band premiered the song while opening for U2 on their U2 360° Tour in May 2011. song was released for airplay on October 8, 2011, and released for download in the United States on iTunes on October 11, 2011.
U218 Singles: U218 Singles is a greatest hits album by the Irish rock band U2, released in November 2006. In most markets, album contains 18 songs. first 16 tracks are 16 of their most successful and popular singles. The seventeenth track is a cover version, collaboration with Green Day, of The Skids' "The Saints Are Coming" to benefit Hurricane Katrina charities. The eighteenth and closing track is a new song called, "Window in the Skies"., in some markets, such as the United Kingdom, an extra song, "I Will Follow" is added to the track list as opening track. " U218 Videos", a DVD featuring music videos from throughout U2's career, was released concurrently.

Laurie Metcalf: Laura Elizabeth "Laurie" Metcalf (born June 16, 1955) is an American actress known for television roles as Jackie Harris on ABC sitcom "Roseanne" (1988–97); Carolyn Bigsby on "Desperate Housewives" (2006); recurring role of Mary Cooper on "The Big Bang Theory" (2007–present); Dr. Jenna James on "Getting On" (2013–15), Marjorie McCarthy in "The McCarthys" (2014–15). voiced role of Mrs. Davis in "Toy Story" film series. other film appearances include "Making Mr. Right" (1987), "JFK" (1991), "Mistress" (1992), as Debbie Salt / Mrs. Loomis in "Scream 2" (1997). She also appeared in commercials for Plan USA, a humanitarian organization helps children in need world.
 Scream (franchise): Scream is an American horror franchise created by Kevin Williamson and Wes Craven. Starring Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, and David Arquette, film series grossed over $604 million in worldwide box-office receipts consists of four motion pictures directed by Craven. first series entry, "Scream", released on December 20, 1996 currently highest-grossing slasher film in United States. second entry "Scream 2" released December 12, 1997 followed by third installment, "Scream 3", released February 4, 2000. Eleven years after previous film, "Scream 4" released on April 15, 2011. films follow Sidney Prescott, her war against succession of murderers who adopt guise of Ghostface to stalk torment victims. Sidney receives support in films from town deputy Dewey Riley, reporter Gale Weathers, and film-geek Randy Meeks. A television spin-off of film series launched by MTV on June 30, 2015. TV series follows different characters and new storylines not connected to film series.
 Timothy Olyphant: Timothy David Olyphant ( ; ; born May 20, 1968) is an American actor and producerHe made acting debut in Off-Broadway theater in 1995 in "The Monogamist", winning Theatre World Award for performance, originated David Sedaris' "The Santaland Diaries" in 1996. Following branched out to film; in early years of career, was often cast in supporting villainous roles, most notably in "Scream 2" (1997), "Go" (1999), "A Man Apart" (2003) and "The Girl Next Door" (2004). came to attention of wider audience with portrayal of Sheriff Seth Bullock in HBO's western "Deadwood" (2004–2006). then had starring roles in romantic comedy "Catch and Release" (2006), action film "Hitman" (2007), thriller "A Perfect Getaway" (2009) and horror film "The Crazies" (2010). was a villain in "Live Free or Die Hard" (2007) and recurring guest star in season two of FX legal thriller "Damages" (2009).
 Rebecca Gayheart: Rebecca Gayheart (born August 12, 1971) is an American fashion model and television and film actress. Gayheart began career appearing in student short film by Brett Ratner, later gained notice as spokesperson and model for Noxzema in early 1990s. had minor roles in "Nothing to Lose" and "Scream 2" (1997) before starring in 1998 slasher film "Urban Legend" (1998) and black comedy "Jawbreaker" (1999). has also had roles on television series "Dead Like Me", "Vanished", and "Nip/Tuck".

Fly540: Five Forty Aviation Ltd, trading as Fly540, is a low-cost airline commenced operations in 2006 based in Nairobi, Kenya, operates domestic and international passenger and freight services. airline had two subsidiary airlines, Fly540 Ghana (suspended in May 2014 and since sold) and Fly540 Angola (suspended in May 2014), but since focused business expansion plans on East Africa.
 Fastjet Tanzania: Fastjet Airlines Limited (Tanzania), also known as Fastjet Tanzania, is low-cost airline operates flights under fastjet brand in Tanzania. airline founded in 2011 as "Fly540 Tanzania", but through acquisition of Fly540 in 2012, rebranded as Fastjet Tanzania. based in Dar es Salaam. airline carried more than 350,000 passengers in first year of operations and sold one million seats by December 2014.
 Teletrol: Teletrol (Teletrol Systems Inc.) is a United States company based in Manchester, New Hampshire. Originally founded in 1981 as Teletrol, Inc., acquired in 1985 by Philips, under continues to operate as a subsidiary. Teletrol is a supplier of building automation systems and components. Its products are designed to centralize management and control of heating/cooling (HVAC) and lighting systems to reduce energy consumption and operating costs for organizations with multiple locations. Teletrol's products consist of hardware components (thermostatic controllers) installed at remote sites, and browser-based software used to communicate between those sites and central location via HTTP.
 Totally Games: Totally Games was an electronic game developer located in Marin County, California. Their titles included X-wing series of games based on Star Wars universe, series of PC-based World War II flight combat simulations (Battlehawks 1942, Their Finest Hour, The Battle of Britain, and Secret Weapons of the Luftwaffe) and "Bridge Commander" based on Star Trek universe. They went on to create Secret Weapons over Normandy in 2003 for the PS2, X-Box and PC.broadened their scope to create products for PSP and Wii (Alien Syndrome) and an interconnected theme park/internet experience, Buzz Lightyear Astroblasters commemorating the 50th anniversary of Disneyland. company was originally founded in 1985 as a sole proprietorship, incorporated in 1993 as Peregrine Software and soon thereafter renamed Totally Games by Lawrence Holland, a Cornell University graduate.
 Goldie & McCulloch: company was originally founded in Galt as Dumfries Foundry in 1844 by James Andrews and James Crombie. exact number of products manufactured by the foundry during this period is unclear, however known that apart from steam engines company also produced safe doors.

Hip hop: Hip hop or hip-hop is a subculture and art movement developed in South Bronx in New York City during late 1970s. people unfamiliar with hip hop culture often use expression "hip hop" to refer exclusively to hip hop music (also called "rap"), Hip hop is characterized by nine distinct elements or expressive realms, of hip hop music is only four elements (rapping, djaying, beatboxing breaking). Afrika Bambaataa of hip hop collective Zulu Nation outlined pillars of hip hop culture, coining terms: "rapping" (also called MCing or emceeing), rhythmic vocal rhyming style (orality); DJing (and turntablism), making music with record players and DJ mixers (aural/sound music creation); b-boying/b-girling/breakdancing (movement/dance); graffiti art, he called "aerosol writin'", many say graffiti hip hop adopted had been around years earlier had nothing to do with hip hop culture. (visual art). Other elements of hip hop subculture arts movements beyond main four are: hip hop culture and historical knowledge of movement (intellectual/philosophical); beatboxing, percussive vocal style; street entrepreneurship; hip hop language; hip hop fashion and style, among others.
 Cyclic Defrost: Cyclic Defrost is an Australian specialist electronic music magazine. founded and edited by Sebastian Chan, with current editors Bob Baker Fish, Chris Downton and Peter Hollo. covers independent electronic music, avant-rock, experimental sound art left field hip hop.
 Experimental hip hop: Experimental hip hop, also known as abstract hip hop, is genre of hip hop employs structural elements typically considered unconventional in traditional hip hop music. notable experimental hip hop record labels include Definitive Jux, Anticon, Big Dada Ninja Tune. most experimental hip hop incorporates turntablism and is produced electronically, some artists introduced acoustic elements to music to facilitate performed live.
List of sound artists: This list of sound artists. Sound art is diverse group of art practices considers wide notions of sound, listening and hearing as predominant focus. contention as to which artists are “sound artists” or if another category more accurate such as experimental music, electronic music, sound installation, circuit bending, sound sculpture, builder of experimental musical instruments, noise music, acoustic ecology, sound poetry, installation art, performance art or Fluxus.
 Sixtoo: Sixtoo was main project of Canadian underground hip hop DJ, producer and rapper Vaughn Robert Squire between 1996 and 2007. He since retired Sixtoo name pursuing other directions in electronic music, with large genre shift from experimental hip hop to deeper club sounds of various tempos. also known as C.L. S.C.A.R.R., Speakerbruiser Rob, and Prison Garde.
 And/oar: and/OAR is an independent record label, based in Seattle, Washington, USA. founded by Dale Lloyd in 2001, officially launched in May 2002. label focuses on raising awareness about field recordings and experimental sound art utilizes field recording as part of creative process. From 2001 to 2005, and/OAR released field recording compilations for Phonography.org a website and international discussion forum pertaining to aspects of "art of field recording". As of December 2014, issued over 70 releases on CD and CD-R formats. From 2008 to 2010, free MP3 releases were made available through website, but this format since discontinued.

Munsonville, New Hampshire: Munsonville unincorporated community in town Nelson Cheshire County, New Hampshire located northwestern corner of Nelson around outlet Granite Lake.
 Nelson, New Hampshire Nelson town in Cheshire County New Hampshire United States population was 729 at 2010 census Nelson includes village Munsonville.
 Buchanan Township, Atchison County, Missouri Buchanan Township one of eleven townships in Atchison County Missouri United States 2010 census population was 83. northwest corner township is northwest corner of entire state.
 Dade County, Georgia: Dade County county in U.S. state Georgia occupies northwest corner of Georgia northwest corner westernmost point in state. 2010 census population 16,633. county seat only incorporated municipality is Trenton.
 Lobster Lake (Maine): Lobster Lake in North Maine Woods named because shape resembles outline of lobster northwest corner lake Northeast Carry township resembles curled lobster tail lake extending eastward into Lobster township resembles lobster thorax larger eastern arm lake southward is "Big Claw" smaller western arm "Little Claw". Lobster Stream connects northwest corner lake to West Branch Penobscot River 1.4 mi north lake Lobster Lake and river similar elevation West Branch may temporarily reverse flow through Lobster Stream into lake during peak runoff events from western Maine highlands Canadian border. lake has self-sustaining populations of native lake trout land-locked Atlantic salmon brook trout populations suppressed by competition from yellow perch and white perch.
Franklin Street Presbyterian Church and Parsonage is historic Presbyterian church at 100 West Franklin Street at Cathedral Street, northwest corner in Baltimore, Maryland, United States church is rectangular Tudor Gothic building dedicated 1847 addition 1865 front features two 60 foot flanking octagonal towers crenelated louvered belfry openings stained glass Gothic-arched windows parsonage has walls of brick heavy Tudor-Gothic window hoods battlements atop roof built 1857 church incorporated 1844 by First Presbyterian Church located northwest corner of East Fayette Street and North Street (now Guilford Avenue) downtown relocated 1854 to West Madison Street and Park Avenue Mount Vernon-Belvedere neighborhood after selling previous third church building 1790-95 to Federal Government built U.S. Courthouse [to 1889 replaced 1932] dedicated 1860 by President James Buchanan). need for new church in fast-growing northern section city formerly "Howard's Woods" of Col. John Eager Howard's (Revolutionary War commander "Maryland Line" regiment Continental Army country estate "Belvedere" (mansion North Calvert and East Chase Streets razed 1875) Washington Monument erected with four surrounding park squares two blocks from new building Franklin Street Church located on "Cathedral Hill" southern part community bordering downtown across street from old Baltimore Cathedral (Basilica of National Shrine of Assumption of Blessed Virgin Mary) erected 1806-1821 designed by Benjamin Latrobe1882-1886 philanthropist Enoch Pratt founded central library for new Enoch Pratt Free Library facing West Mulberry Street at Cathedral, block south replaced 1931-33 by new central library building encompassing entire block now across Franklin Street from F.S.P.C. 1973 two historic congregations reunited to form First and Franklin Street Presbyterian Church centered at First Church site on West Madison and Park. Franklin Street building used by merged congregation for time sold to fundamentalist independent Protestant congregation later re-sold to present "New Unity Church Ministries". Across Cathedral Street northeast was 1820s era Greek Revival home designed by Robert Mills (who did Washington Monument two blocks away) occupied by original Maryland Club, exclusive Southern-leaning dining and leisure society of gentlemen founded 1857 threatened by Massachusetts Militia Gen. Benjamin F. Butler, U.S.A. occupied Baltimore beginning Civil War on May 13, 1861 fortified Federal Hill with Fort and cannons overlooking harbor and city rebel flag flying discontent declared martial law Club moved to North Charles and East Eager Streets in 1892 mansion replaced by former Central Building of Young Men's Christian Association of Central Maryland (YMCA) closed in 1980s building renovated as Mount Vernon Hotel and Cafe.

A Pair of Brown Eyes: "A Pair of Brown Eyes" is a single by The Pogues, released on 18 March 1985. single was their first to make UK Top 100, peaking at Number 72. It featured on the band's second album, "Rum Sodomy & the Lash", composed by Pogues front man Shane MacGowan, on the melody of "Wild Mountain Thyme", also known as "Will Ye Go Lassie Go," a song by Francis McPeake in traditional Irish folk style.
 A Spanner in the Works: The album includes covers of Bob Dylan's "Sweetheart Like You" and The Blue Nile's "The Downtown Lights". The song "Muddy, Sam, And Otis", is tribute to Muddy Waters, Sam Cooke, and Otis Redding. Track 12, later released as a single featuring the Scottish Euro '96 Football Squad, "Purple Heather" is a folk song normally goes by the name "Wild Mountain Thyme". often credited as traditional, but was written by The McPeakes. "Leave Virginia Alone" was written by Tom Petty and recorded for his album "Wildflowers", but left off finished album and given to Stewart instead.
 Wild Mountain Thyme: "Wild Mountain Thyme" (also known as "Purple Heather" and "Will Ye Go, Lassie, Go?") is a Scottish folk song collected by Francis McPeake 1st, who wrote song himself for his wife. The McPeake family claim recognition for the writing of song. Francis McPeake is a member of a well known musical family in Belfast, Northern Ireland. lyrics and melody are a variant of song "The Braes of Balquhither" by Scottish poet Robert Tannahill (1774–1810), a contemporary of Robert Burns. Tannahill's original song, first published in Robert Archibald Smith's "Scottish Minstrel" (1821–24), is about hills ("braes") around Balquhidder near Lochearnhead.Like Burns, Tannahill collected and adapted traditional songs, "The Braes of Balquhither" may have been based on traditional song "The Braes o' Bowhether".
 Brown Eyes (song): "Brown Eyes" is a song by Fleetwood Mac from 1979 double LP "Tusk". It was one of six songs written and sung by Christine McVie. Original guitarist Peter Green also took part in the sessions for "Brown Eyes", but his playing on track is not credited on album. Due to his deteriorating health in the 70s, Green admitted in 1999 he had no recollection of this contribution. "Brown Eyes" also performed on Mirage Tour and Shakin the Cage tour.
 Brown Eyes (band): Brown Eyes (Korean: 브라운아이즈) is a South Korean male duo consisting of members, Yoon Gun and Naul. Brown Eyes released their first album, "Brown Eyes" on June 7, 2001.
 Beautiful Brown Eyes: "Beautiful Brown Eyes" is a traditional country song arranged by Fiddlin' Arthur Smith & Alton Delmore of The Delmore Brothers in 1951. An award presented to Alton Delmore for "Beautiful Brown Eyes" in 1951.
 Caramel (City High song): "Caramel" is second single released from American R&B/hip hop trio City High's self-titled debut album in 2001. song was written based on the appearance and personality of Brian Gough, though he is actually 5'6" with brown eyes not 5'5" with brown eyes. It is the group's second most successful single, peaking at number 18 on "Billboard" Hot 100 and number nine on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Singles & Tracks in the U.S. in January 2002.

Kurt Vonnegut: Kurt Vonnegut Jr. ( ; November 11, 1922April 11, 2007) was an American writer. In career spanning over 50 years, Vonnegut published 14 novels, three short story collections, five plays, five works of non-fiction. most famous for his darkly satirical best-selling novel "Slaughterhouse-Five" (1969).
 Armageddon in Retrospect: Armageddon in Retrospect is collection of short stories and essays about war and peace written by Kurt Vonnegut. first posthumous collection of his previously unpublished writings. book includes introduction by Mark Vonnegut, letter from Kurt to his family about experiences as American prisoner of war in Nazi Germany, fire-bombing of Dresden. Like Vonnegut's other books, "Armageddon in Retrospect" is laden with handwritten quotations rough drawings by author.
 Jaroslav Hašek: Jaroslav Hašek (] ; April 30, 1883 – January 3, 1923) was Czech writer, humorist, satirist, journalist, bohemian anarchist. best known for his novel "The Good Soldier Švejk", unfinished collection of farcical incidents about soldier in World War I satire on ineptitude of authority figures. novel translated into about 60 languages, making it most translated novel in Czech literature. also known as the Obscure Czech Writer.
 Joanna Russ: Joanna Russ (February 22, 1937 – April 29, 2011) was an American writer, academic radical feminist. author of works of science fiction, fantasy feminist literary criticism as "How to Suppress Women's Writing", contemporary novel, "On Strike Against God", one children's book, "Kittatinny". best known for "The Female Man", novel combining utopian fiction and satire, and story "When It Changed".
 Hugh Gallagher (humorist): Hugh Gallagher is an author and musician from New York City.best known for his satire, including his band Von Von Von, award-winning satire on college application essay, "3A Essay", and novel "Teeth".
 The Magic Christian (novel): The Magic Christian is a 1959 comic novel by American author Terry Southern (1924–1995) about an odd billionaire spends of time playing elaborate practical jokes on people known for bringing Southern to attention of filmmaker Stanley Kubrick, who received a copy as a gift from Peter Sellers, hired him as co-writer for "Dr. Strangelove" (1964) when Kubrick decided to make film a black comedy/satire, rather than straightforward thriller. In 1969, "The Magic Christian" made into film starring Peter Sellers and Ringo Starr; story altered and relocated from New York City to London.
 Little Big Man (novel): Little Big Man is a 1964 novel by American author Thomas Berger. Often described as satire or parody of western genre, book is modern example of picaresque fiction. Berger made use of large volume of overlooked first-person primary materials, as diaries, letters, and memoirs, to fashion wide-ranging entertaining tale comments on alienation, identity, and perceptions of reality. Berger's best known work, "Little Big Man" made into a popular film by Arthur Penn. called "Berger's response to great American myth of the frontier, representing most of central traditions of American literature."

Sarod: The sarod (or sarode) (सरोद) is a stringed instrument of India, used mainly in Indian classical music. Along with the sitar, it among most popular and prominent instruments in Hindustani classical music. sarod is known for a deep, weighty, introspective sound, in contrast with sweet, overtone-rich texture of sitar, with sympathetic strings give it resonant, reverberant quality. It is a fretless instrument to produce continuous slides between notes known as meend (glissandi), important in Indian music.
 Apratim Majumdar: Apratim Majumdar (born 1978), is an Indian classical musician from Kolkata, India. He plays the Sarod. His "Dhrupadee Veenkar" style of Ustad Alauddin Khan's Seni Veenkar Gharana: analytically imaginative prosodic progression with metrical waves of melodic phrases interwoven with highest technical brilliance and maturity reminds great legends of the Gharana. He is an internationally recognized instructor of classical Indian music.
 Sousaphone: The sousaphone ( ), is a brass instrument in the same family as the widely known tuba. Created around 1893 by J.W. Pepper at direction of American bandleader John Philip Sousa (whom instrument was then named after), it designed to be easier to play than concert tuba while standing or marching, to carry sound of instrument above heads of band. Like the tuba, sound is produced by moving air past lips, causing them to vibrate or "buzz" into a large cupped mouthpiece. Unlike tuba, instrument is bent in a circle to fit around the body of musician; ends in a large, flaring bell pointed forward, projecting sound ahead of player. Because of ease of carrying and direction of sound, it widely employed in marching bands, various other musical genres.Sousaphones originally made out of brass but mid-20th century started to be made from lighter materials like fiberglass; today both types in wide use.
 Experimental musical instrument: experimental musical instrument (or custom-made instrument) is musical instrument modifies or extends existing instrument or class of instruments, or defines or creates new class of instrument. Some created through simple modifications, such as cracked drum cymbals or metal objects inserted between piano strings in prepared piano. Some experimental instruments created from household items like homemade mute for brass instruments such as bathtub plugs. Other experimental instruments created from electronic spare parts, or by mixing acoustic instruments with electric components.
 Accompaniment: Accompaniment is musical parts provide rhythmic and/or harmonic support for melody or main themes of song or instrumental piece. many different styles and types of accompaniment in different genres and styles of music. In homophonic music, main accompaniment approach used in popular music, clear vocal melody supported by subordinate chords. In popular music and traditional music, accompaniment parts provide "beat" for music and outline chord progression of song or instrumental piece. accompaniment for vocal melody or instrumental solo can be played by single musician playing instrument such as piano, pipe organ, or guitar. any instrument can in theory be used as accompaniment instrument, keyboard and guitar-family instruments tend to be used if only a single instrument, as these instruments can play chords and basslines simultaneously (chords and bassline easier to play simultaneously on keyboard instruments, but fingerpicking guitarist can play chords and a bassline simultaneously on guitar). solo singer can accompany herself by playing guitar or piano while she sings, and in some rare cases, solo singer can even accompany himself or herself just using his or her voice and body (e.g., Bobby McFerrin).

Winnie the Pooh (song): "Winnie the Pooh" is the title song for the franchise of same name. It is musically emblematic of most successful branding Disney owns and used in most merchandising models of brand since song's first publication in 1966 in the musical film featurette "Winnie the Pooh and the Honey Tree". In film, song is generally utilized in the title sequence. lyric gives overview of characters and roles each plays in relation to Pooh himself. song used in every theatrically released Pooh film most of television series. songwriters are the Sherman Brothers, written the grand majority of Winnie the Pooh songs and musical numbers since 1966. unknown who performed the song. song was also performed by Carly Simon. A music video was released for this version and included in "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh" DVD.
 The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers: "The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers" is the theme song and personal anthem of Tigger, a fictional tiger from the children's book series Winnie-the-Pooh. Tigger's birthday is believed to be in October 1928, the year "The House at Pooh Corner" was first published, on Tigger-related merchandise, Disney often indicates Tigger's birth year as 1968, a reference to the first year Tigger appeared in a Disney production, "Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day". That also the same instance when Tigger first sang this song. song repeated in Disney's 1974 release "Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Too! ", The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh ride and then again in the 1977 release "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh". "The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers" opens up the 2000 release of "The Tigger Movie". In 1974, Paul Winchell earned a Grammy for his rendition of the song.
Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day: Winnie the Pooh and Blustery Day is a 1968 animated featurette based on third, fifth, ninth, and tenth chapters from "Winnie-the-Pooh" and second, eighth, and ninth chapters from "The House at Pooh Corner" by A. A. Milne. featurette produced by Walt Disney Productions released by Buena Vista Distribution Company on December 20, 1968 as a double feature with "The Horse in the Gray Flannel Suit". This was the second of the studio's Winnie the Pooh shorts. later added as a segment to the 1977 film "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh". music written by Richard M. Sherman and Robert B. Sherman. notable for being last animated short produced by Walt Disney, who died during its production.
 Up, Down and Touch the Ground: "Up, Down and Touch the Ground" is a song from the 1966 musical film featurette "Winnie the Pooh and the Honey Tree". song also subsequently incorporated into the 1977 musical film, "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh" which is an amalgamation of three previous Winnie-the-Pooh featurettes including "The Honey Tree". In the song Winnie the Pooh's exercise makes him hungry, he over-eats (it leads to his stuck-in-Rabbit's door incident later in the film), proud of his fat stomach exercises to gain weight and grow rounder. Halfway through song, he bends down too far, accidentally ripping the stitching on his bottom as result of becoming fat, but upon seeing his bottom in mirror, quickly ties it together again. By end of song Pooh rationalized his over-eating by calling his hunger, "healthy".

Berger Blanc Suisse: The Berger Blanc Suisse (English: White Swiss Shepherd , German: "Weisser Schweizer Schäferhund" , Italian: "Pastore Svizzero Bianco" ) is a breed of dog from Switzerland. It of same origins as the White Shepherd and the German Shepherd Dog, and recognized as a separate breed by the FCI.
 Pandikona: The Pandikona is a primitive-type hunting dog from Pattikonda taluk-Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh state, India. "Pandikona" is a medium size sight hound adapted to harsh climatic conditions of Kurnool district. This breed is associated with shepherd families of that region. PandiKona dogs need little care.
 Prosthetic Neuronal Memory Silicon Chips: Prosthetic Neuronal Memory Silicon Chip is a device that imitates the brain's process of creating long-term memories. device was designed by Theodore Berger, a Biomedical Engineer and Neurologist at University of Southern California. Berger started to work on this chip in the early 1990s. He and his colleagues have able to implant electrodes into rats and monkeys that restore their memories after previously being impaired. While researchers are well into developing an actual memory prosthesis in animals, they still need to show their chips can form long-term memories in many different behavioral situations. Berger hopes to eventually use these chips as electronic implants for humans whose brains that suffer from diseases such as Alzheimer's that disrupt neuronal networks.
 Tentacle: In zoology, a tentacle is a flexible, mobile, elongated organ present in some species of animals, most of them invertebrates. In animal anatomy, tentacles usually occur in one or more pairs. Anatomically, tentacles of animals work mainly like muscular hydrostats. Most forms of tentacles are used for grasping and feeding. Many are sensory organs, variously receptive to touch, vision, or to the smell or taste of particular foods or threats. Examples of such tentacles are the "eye stalks" of various kinds of snails.Some kinds of tentacles have both sensory and manipulatory functions.
 Ticks of domestic animals: Ticks of domestic animals cause poor health and loss of production to their hosts by many parasitic mechanisms. Ticks also transmit numerous of viruses, bacteria, and protozoa between domestic animals. These microbes cause diseases can be severely debilitating or fatal to domestic animals, and may also affect humans. Ticks are especially important to domestic animals in tropical and subtropical countries, where warm climate enables many species of ticks to flourish., the large populations of wild animals in warm countries provide a reservoir of ticks and infective microbes that spread to domestic animals. Farmers of livestock animals use many methods to control ticks, and related treatments are used to reduce infestation of companion animals. Veterinarians and animal health agencies work at private, national, and international scales to reduce the harm caused by ticks and their associated diseases.

Classical realism (international relations): Classical Realism is a theory of International Relations established in post-World War II era seeks to explain international politics as result of human nature. theory is associated with thinkers Niccolò Machiavelli and Thomas Hobbes. Modern thinkers associated with classical realism are Carl von Clausewitz, Hans Morgenthau Reinhold Niebuhr. Classical Realist thought overshadowed by Neorealism after Kenneth Waltz' work became widely accepted due to rise of Structuralism in North American International Relations scholarship favored latter's emphasis on rationality rather than human nature as cause for political conflict.
 On War: Vom Kriege (] ) is a book on war and military strategy by Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz (1780–1831), written mostly after Napoleonic wars, between 1816 and 1830, published posthumously by his wife Marie von Brühl in 1832. translated into English several times as On War. "On War" is an unfinished work; Clausewitz had set about revising his accumulated manuscripts in 1827, but did not live to finish task. His wife edited his collected works and published them between 1832 and 1835. His 10-volume collected works contain most of his larger historical and theoretical writings, not his shorter articles and papers or his extensive correspondence with important political, military, intellectual and cultural leaders in Prussian state. "On War" is formed by the first three volumes and represents his theoretical explorations. It is one of the most important treatises on political-military analysis and strategy ever written, and remains both controversial and an influence on strategic thinking.
 Absolute war: The concept of absolute war was a theoretical construct developed by Prussian military theorist General Carl von Clausewitz in his famous but unfinished philosophical exploration of war, "Vom Kriege" (in English, "On War", 1832). It is discussed only in first half of Book VIII (there only a couple of references to it elsewhere) does not appear in sections of the text written later.This indicates experiment failed and meant to be dropped.
 August Otto Rühle von Lilienstern: August Otto Rühle von Lilienstern, born 1780, died 1847. Prussian officer, joined Scharnhorst's Academy for Officers in the same class as Carl von Clausewitz. Later they both taught at Prussian General War School, would become the Prussian War Academy, and Rühle became Clausewitz' second successor as its director. Rühle published many articles, kept official war diaries, and wrote a two-volume "Manual for the Officer for Education in Peace and for Use in Action" ("Handbuch für den Offizier zur Belehrung im Frieden und zum Gebrauch im Felde"), published in Berlin in 1817 and 1818. Lilienstern and Clausewitz, teaching at the same school at time of publication of this manual, were in agreement on many points. For example, they agreed war was political in nature (which neither novel nor controversial idea) and war was a "Zweikampf." (That, literally a "two-struggle," usually translated into English as "duel," though in fact imagery and metaphor Clausewitz pursued was a wrestling match.) Clausewitz made these ideas famous in his book On War. Their common views on such issues can be traced to the nature of military intellectual community in Prussia and common influence of Scharnhorst.

Hawker Hurricane: The Hawker Hurricane is a British single-seat fighter aircraft of the 1930s–1940s that was designed and predominantly built by Hawker Aircraft Ltd for the Royal Air Force (RAF).  Although overshadowed by the Supermarine Spitfire, the aircraft became renowned during the Battle of Britain, accounting for 60 percent of the RAF air victories in the battle, and served in all the major theatres of the Second World War.

No. 1455 Flight RAF: No. 1455 (Fighter) Flight was formed at RAF Tangmere, West Sussex on 7 July 1941, equipped with Turbinlite Douglas Boston and Douglas Havoc aircraft.  On operations they co-operated with the Hawker Hurricanes of 1 Squadron and 3 Squadron.  The flight was replaced with 534 Squadron on 2 September 1942.

Battle of Britain Memorial Flight: The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight (BBMF) is a Royal Air Force flight which provides an aerial display group usually comprising an Avro Lancaster, a Supermarine Spitfire and a Hawker Hurricane.  The aircraft are regularly seen at events commemorating the Second World War and upon British State occasions, notably Trooping the Colour, celebrating Queen Elizabeth II's 80th birthday in 2006, as well as the wedding of Prince William, Duke of Cambridge and Catherine Middleton in 2011 and at air displays throughout the United Kingdom and Europe.

Supermarine Seafire: The Supermarine Seafire was a naval version of the Supermarine Spitfire adapted for operation from aircraft carriers.  In concept, it is relatively comparable to the Hawker Sea Hurricane, a navalised version of the Spitfire's stablemate, the Hawker Hurricane.  The name Seafire had been derived from the abbreviation of the longer name Sea Spitfire.

Flying Legend Hawker Hurricane Replica: The Flying Legend Hawker Hurricane Replica is an Italian light-sport aircraft, designed and produced by Flying Legend of Caltagirone and introduced at the AERO Friedrichshafen show in 2011.  The aircraft, a 72% scale replica of the British Hawker Hurricane Second World War fighter, is supplied as a kit for amateur construction or as a complete ready-to-fly-aircraft.

Real Thing (Norwegian band): Real Thing (1992-1995) Soul Jazz Band from Oslo, Norway founded 1992 Sigurd Køhn Palle Wagnberg formed forerunner The B3 Blues Band with Vidar Busk Hamlet Pedersen changed name when Staffan William-Olsson Fredrik Carl Stormer joined band Størmer replaced by Torstein Ellingsen in 1995 Ellingsen by Børre Dalhaug in 1998. Due to sudden death of band saxophonist Sigurd Køhn in December 2004 Real Thing hibernating until reunion 2010.
 Torstein Ellingsen (born 7 August 1966) Norwegian drummer music producer known from album recordings.
 Norwegians: Norwegians Germanic ethnic group native to Norway share common culture speak Norwegian language Norwegian people descendants found in migrant communities worldwide United States Canada Australia Argentina Chile Uruguay Brazil Mexico New Zealand United Kingdom South Africa
 Turkish people: Turkish people known as Anatolian Turks "Anadolu Türkleri" Turkic ethnic group nation living mainly in Turkey speaking Turkish most spoken Turkic language largest ethnic group in Turkey largest ethnic group among speakers of Turkic languages. Ethnic Turkish minorities exist in former lands Ottoman Empire Turkish diaspora established with modern migration in Western Europe.
 Fezara people: Fezara ethnic group of Sudan emigrated from Arabia to Egypt Sudan number persons group about 200,000. Most members are Muslims speaks Sudanese Arabic.
Ewe people: Ewe people (Ewe "Eʋeawó" lit "Ewe people"; or " Eʋedukɔ́ " "Ewe nation","Eʋenyigba" Eweland are African ethnic group largest in Togo (32%) third largest in Ghana (14%) minority in southern Benin Ivory Coast Nigeria speak Ewe language (Ewe "Eʋegbe" ) Niger-Congo family languages related to other speakers Gbe languages Fon, Gen Phla Phera Aja people of Togo Benin.
 Konkomba people: Gur ethnic group residing in Northern Brong Ahafo Volta Eastern Greater Accra Regions of Ghana. Saboba Chereponi Nanumba Districts Gushiegu Karaga districts Zabzugu Tatale-Sanguli districts Northern Nkwanta North South Districts Volta Region administrative districts where Bikpakpaam seen populations Other key towns of Bikpakpaam Ghana are Atebubu, Kintampo Techiman Yeji in Brong Ahafo Region Act 280 Anatomy act of Ghana Konkomba people (known as Bikpakpaam second largest ethnic group in Northern Region Ghana 2010 census data Bikpakpaam Ghana number 823,000 intercensal growth rate population more than one million World Factbook reports Konkomba people 8th largest Ethnic group in Ghana 3.5% of Total population Ghana Saboba (Chabob) Northern Region Ghana capital town of all Bikpakpaam Bikpakpaam also found in republic Togo, sister West African country to GhanaTogo Bikpakpaam reside Kara Central Plateaux Regions. Guerin Kouka Nanguem Do capital of Dankpen district) in Kara Region capital town of Bikpakpaam Togo Dankpen district north western corridor Togo Schwartz's (2005) account Bikpakpaam number about 50,100 in Togo 2011 census Togo indicates total population Bikpakpaam in Dankpen district 122,209. Visit Konkomba language for information Konkomba people speak Konkomba language Likpakpaln. traditional dance is Kinachunŋ (pronounced k-i-naa-chung). Konkomba settlements led by traditional chief Ubor. In Bikpakpaam dominant areas people instituted established own chieftains overlords Saboba area has Uchabob-bor as overlord. Bikpakpaam believe in solidarity determination hard-work Until 21st primary occupation was farming animal husbandry Bikpakpaam mainly subsistence farmers rearers of animals poultry small ruminants cattle explains scattered settlement across West African sub-region Maasole intimates Bikpakpaam always on move search for fertile farmlands. Most Konkombas actively in education research projects Konkombas become dominant force in politics health education civil society by 2025.

Sasanian Empire: Sasanian Empire ( also known as Sassanian, Sasanid, Sassanid or Neo-Persian Empire, known to inhabitants as Ērānshahr in Middle Persian, was last period of Persian Empire (Iran) before rise of Islam named after House of Sasan ruled from 224 to 651 AD. Sasanian Empire succeeded Parthian Empire recognised as one of leading world powers alongside Roman-Byzantine Empire for more than 400 years.
 Farrukhzad Khosrow V: Farrukhzad Khosrau V was briefly king of Sasanian Empire from March 631 to April 631. son of Khosrau II.
 Samo: Samo founded first recorded political union of Slavic tribes, known as Samo's Empire ("realm", "tribal union"), from Silesia to present-day Slovenia ruling from 623 until death in 658. According to Fredegarius Samo was Frankish merchant unified Slavic tribes against robber raids and violence by Avars showing bravery command skills in battle elected as "Slavic king" (Latin: "Rex Sclavorum" ). In 631 Samo defended realm against Frankish Kingdom in three-day Battle of Wogastisburg.
 Samo's Empire: Samo's Empire is historiographical name for Slavic tribal union established by King ("rex") Samo existed between 631 and 658 A.D.. centre of union was likely in Moravia union included Silesia, Bohemia, Lusatia and Carantania.
Duchy of Thuringia: Duchy of Thuringia was an eastern frontier march of Merovingian kingdom of Austrasia, established about 631 by King Dagobert I after his troops defeated by forces Slavic confederation of Samo at Battle of Wogastisburg. recreated in Carolingian Empire dukes appointed by king until absorbed by Saxon dukes in 908. From about 1111/12 territory was ruled by Landgraves of Thuringia as Princes of Holy Roman Empire.
 Khosrow IV: Khosrow IV was a Sasanian usurper ruled briefly in 631. Little known about his rule appears to ruled during time of upheaval and chaos across Sasanian Empire 7th century century where Iran plunged into "dark ages". was son of Mah-Adhur Gushnasp, minister of Sasanian Empire during reign of Ardashir III, and Kahar-dukht, daughter of Yazdandar, son of Khosrau I. His rule seems to coincide with other pretenders Hormizd VI likely he ruled a district or province rather than Empire in entirety. killed after few days of reign.

Stone Brewing Co.: Stone Brewing is a brewery headquartered in Escondido, California, USA. Founded in 1996 in San Marcos, California, is the largest brewery in Southern California. Based on 2016 sales volume the ninth largest craft brewery in United States.
 Beer Wars: Beer Wars is a 2009 documentary film about American beer industry., covers differences between large corporate breweries, Anheuser-Busch, Miller Brewing Company, and Coors Brewing Company opposed to smaller breweries like Dogfish Head Brewery, Moonshot 69, Yuengling, Stone Brewing Co., and other producers of craft beer. Also covered is how advertising and lobbyists are used to control beer market, implying harm competition and consumer choice.
 Microbrewery: A microbrewery or craft brewery is brewery produces small amounts of beer (or sometimes root beer), typically smaller than large-scale corporate breweries, and is independently owned. Such breweries characterized by emphasis on quality, flavour and brewing technique.
 List of breweries in California: This list of breweries in California, current and defunct, includes microbreweries and larger industrial scale breweries. Brewing companies range widely in volume and variety of beer produced, ranging from small breweries to massive multinational conglomerates. Since 1983, California has allowed breweries to sell beer on their premises, giving rise to numerous brewpubs and microbreweries.
 Brouwerij 't IJ: Brouwerij 't IJ (] ; English: The IJ Brewery) is a small brewery in Amsterdam, Netherlands. located in a former bath house named "Funen", next to the De Gooyer windmill. brewery opened by Kaspar Peterson, a former musician, in October 1985 and was one of several small breweries opened in cities around Netherlands in response to consumers' dissatisfaction with beer brewed by larger companies. It brews eight standard beers and three seasonal beers, besides limited edition beers.
 Beer by region: This is list of articles and categories dealing with beer by region, including breweries and brewing in general. Beer is world's most widely consumed alcoholic beverage, third-most popular drink overall, after water and tea. thought by to the oldest fermented beverage. A brewery is a dedicated building for making of beer, though beer can be made at home, has been for much of beer's history. A company that makes beer is called either a brewery or a brewing company. diversity of size in breweries is matched by diversity of processes, degrees of automation, and kinds of beer produced in breweries. A brewery is typically divided into distinct sections, with each section reserved for one part of brewing process.

2016–17 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2016–17 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2016–17 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. Gaels, led by seventh year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletic Center in New Rochelle, New York as members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference (MAAC). finished season 22–13, 12–8 in MAAC play to finish in a tie for third place. defeated Rider, Saint Peter's and Siena to be champions of the MAAC Tournament. received MAAC's automatic bid to NCAA Tournament lost in the First Round to Oregon.
 2010–11 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2010–11 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2010–11 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. Gaels, led by first year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletics Center members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference. finished season 25–12, 13–5 in MAAC and lost in championship game of 2011 MAAC Men's Basketball Tournament to Saint Peter's. invited to 2011 CollegeInsider.com Tournament advanced to championship game before falling to Santa Clara.
 2011–12 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2011–12 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2011–12 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. Gaels, led by second year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletic Center members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference. Gaals were MAAC regular season champions but failed to win MAAC Basketball Tournament after losing to Fairfield in semifinals. received at–large bid to the 2012 NCAA Tournament lost to BYU in "First Four" round. Gaels led BYU by 25 points in 2nd half. It was the largest comeback in NCAA Tournament history.
2013–14 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2013–14 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2013–14 NCAA Division I men's basketball season Gaels, led by fourth year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at Hynes Athletic Center were members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference. finished season 22–11, 17–3 to win MAAC regular season championship. advanced to championship game of MAAC Tournament lost to Manhattan. As a regular season conference champion who failed to win their conference tournament, received automatic bid to National Invitation Tournament lost in first round to Louisiana Tech.
 2015–16 Iona Gaels men's basketball team: 2015–16 Iona Gaels men's basketball team represented Iona College during 2015–16 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. Gaels, led by sixth year head coach Tim Cluess, played home games at the Hynes Athletic Center were members of Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference (MAAC). finished season 22–11, 16–4 in MAAC play to finish in second place. defeated Canisius, Siena, and Monmouth to be champions of MAAC Tournament and earn the conference's automatic bid to NCAA Tournament where, as a #13 seed, lost in the first round to Iowa State.

Russian Revolution: The Russian Revolution was a pair of revolutions in Russia in 1917 dismantled Tsarist autocracy and led to rise of Soviet Union. Russian Empire collapsed with abdication of Emperor Nicholas II and old regime was replaced by provisional government during first revolution of February 1917 (March in the Gregorian calendar; older Julian calendar was in use in Russia at time). Alongside it arose grassroots community assemblies (called 'soviets') contended for authority. In the second revolution that October, Provisional Government was toppled and all power was given to soviets.
 Russia–United Kingdom relations: Russia–United Kingdom relations (Russian: Российско-британские отношения ) is relationship between the Russian Federation and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and it's overseas territories. Spanning nearly five centuries, it often switched from state of alliance to rivalry or even war.
